119jnw: This week you review two classes that go together: how to tell whether a word is masculine or feminine, and which article to choose depending on what the other person knows. One idea guides everything: **learn every word with its article**.
qprzn7: The ending gives you a clue
2atu5a: Look at the end of the word. Masculine words almost always end in **-o** or **-or**: _el vaso_, _el color_, _el ascensor_. Feminine words almost always end in **-a**: _la plaza_.
hyi20k: Some endings are very reliable: **-ción**, **-sión**, **-dad** and **-tad** are always feminine: _la estación_, _la televisión_, _la ciudad_, _la libertad_.
10kb8pd: With **-e** or other consonants there's no rule: _el puente_, _la calle_, _el árbol_, _la sal_. Here only memory works: word and article together.
lcmdvd: A famous -or exception: **la flor**. Learn it with a picture: a red flower on the table.
3jxv42: Some common words are deceptive. They end in -a and are masculine: _el día_, _el mapa_, _el tema_, _el idioma_, _el sistema_. They end in -o and are feminine: _la mano_, _la foto_, _la moto_, _la radio_.
3fuzf0: But not every word ending in **-ma** is masculine: _la cama_, _la crema_, _la forma_ are feminine. So, once again: word and article together.
1fwfexa: Special case: some feminine words begin with a strong (stressed) **a**: _agua_, _aula_, _área_. In the singular they take **el** or **un** for the sound, but they stay feminine: _el agua fría_. In the plural they go back to **las**: _las aulas_.
9o53fz: _Tema_ is a trap: it ends in -a, but it's masculine.
1s1wl0s: _Agua_ begins with a stressed a: in the singular, **el** agua.
1xisas0: _El_ is only for the sound: _agua_ is feminine, and so is the adjective.
16nba8b: Use **un, una, unos, unas** when you introduce something **new** in the conversation: the other person doesn't know which one yet. _Hay un mercado en el centro._
1hx5p9f: **Hay** almost always goes with un/una (or nothing, or a number): _Hay una parada aquí_, _Hay dos bancos_. Never _hay el_ or _hay la_.
135cnp5: You also use un/una to say **what something is like**: _Guadalajara es una ciudad grande_.
u9dh0m: El, la: we already know which one
1c50b7a: Use **el, la, los, las** when both people know **which one** it is: because you've already mentioned it, because it's unique or because it's right there in the situation.
c65nrn: It's the natural flow of a story: first _un_, then _el_. _Hay una plaza con una fuente. La plaza es antigua y la fuente es enorme._
1gl4wqd: The key question isn't “does it exist?”, but “does the other person know which one it is?”. In a hotel, _¿Dónde está el ascensor?_: there's only one, and you both know it.
11qhu0c: Listen to a story in Spanish and count: how many times does it go from _un_ to _el_? It's the most common pattern.
3ww5ah: Second mention: we already know which fountain it is, **la** fuente.
l7fgfq: The exit of this building is a specific one: **la**.

f8bohc: Every Spanish word has one **stressed syllable**: it's said with a little more force. In _mercado_ it's **CA**: mer-**CA**-do. If you move the stress, the word sounds strange or changes its meaning.
7p4c7y: The general rule: if the word ends in a vowel, -n or -s, the stress falls on the second to last syllable (_pla-za_, _ca-lle_). If it ends in another consonant, on the last one (_co-lor_, _ciu-dad_). If it doesn't follow the rule, it has a written **accent**: _es-ta-ción_, _ár-bol_.
nh2r9d: The stressed syllable explains _el agua_: the voice lands on the first **a** (**A**-gua). In _alarma_ the stress is on _LAR_, so we say _la alarma_.
1nth92h: The written accent marks the stressed syllable when the word doesn't follow the rule: _televisión_, _árbol_, _panadería_. In the plural the accent sometimes disappears: _estación → estaciones_.
djfc7v: Stress on the first **a** of each word: **A**-gua, **AU**-la, **Á**-rea.
i3jici: Here the first a is weak: a-**LAR**-ma, a-**YU**-da. That's why it's _la_.
1a9gr0j: The stress doesn't move: es-ta-**CIÓN**, es-ta-**CIO**-nes.
121k162: mer-**CA**-do, **CEN**-tro: second to last, because they end in a vowel.
f03ds3: ciu-**DAD**, ca-te-**DRAL**: they end in a consonant, so the stress goes at the end.
